reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: Onycholysis is separation of the nail plate from the underlying nail bed, usually starting distally or laterally and creating a whitish or yellowish air-filled space
It is a sign, not a diagnosis, so the priority is to identify the underlying cause rather than simply treat the loosened nail
Psoriasis is a very common cause and is often accompanied by pitting, oil-drop discolouration, and subungual hyperkeratosis
Repeated mechanical or chemical trauma, including aggressive manicuring and prolonged wet work, is a frequent and overlooked trigger
Thyroid dysfunction, especially hyperthyroidism, can produce distal separation known as Plummer's nail
Photo-onycholysis follows exposure to certain photosensitising drugs (for example tetracyclines and some psoralens) after sunlight and typically affects several nails
The exposed nail bed loses its protective seal and becomes vulnerable to secondary colonisation by yeasts and Pseudomonas, the latter giving a greenish tinge
Management is directed at the cause, keeping the nail short and dry, minimising trauma and wet exposure, and treating any secondary infection
reference.pathophysiology: Onycholysis arises when the bonds anchoring the keratinised nail plate to the epithelium of the nail bed are disrupted, so that the plate lifts away and an air-filled space forms beneath it. The separation may be driven by inflammatory disease of the nail bed such as psoriasis, by repeated mechanical or chemical injury, by a phototoxic reaction to circulating drugs, or by systemic influences such as altered thyroid hormone levels. Once the seal between plate and bed is broken, keratin debris, moisture, and micro-organisms accumulate in the subungual space, and secondary colonisation with yeasts or Pseudomonas can perpetuate the problem and alter the colour of the nail.
additionalDifferentials: Nail psoriasis with associated pitting and subungual hyperkeratosis
Traumatic or occupational nail bed damage
Contact irritant or allergic reactions to nail cosmetics and adhesives
additionalInvestigations: Careful history for trauma, wet work, cosmetics, and photosensitising medication
Nail clipping and subungual scrapings for mycology to confirm or exclude fungal infection
Onychoscopy (dermoscopy of the nail) to characterise the pattern and margin of separation
Thyroid function tests when a systemic cause is suspected
Swab of the subungual space if greenish discolouration suggests Pseudomonas
Assessment for cutaneous psoriasis or other skin disease elsewhere on the body
redFlags: Separation confined to a single nail with an underlying mass, suggesting a subungual tumour
Associated pigmentation or bleeding raising the possibility of subungual melanoma
Rapidly spreading discolouration or pain indicating secondary infection
Persistent unexplained onycholysis unresponsive to removal of obvious triggers
reference.prognosis: Onycholysis usually resolves once the underlying cause is corrected and the nail is allowed to grow out attached, but recovery is slow because it depends on outgrowth of new plate, and persistent triggers such as psoriasis or continued trauma lead to relapse.
pitfalls: Assuming all onycholysis is fungal and prescribing antifungals without confirmatory mycology
Overlooking a photosensitising drug when several nails are affected after sun exposure
Failing to recognise a single stubborn separated nail as a marker of an underlying tumour
Encouraging cleaning under the nail, which extends the space and worsens the separation
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
management: Identify and remove the underlying cause as the priority, since onycholysis is a sign rather than a diagnosis
Clip away the detached portion of plate and keep the subungual space dry to allow the new nail to reattach as it grows out
Avoid mechanical and chemical triggers, including aggressive manicuring, prolonged wet work and irritant cosmetics
Treat nail psoriasis with topical corticosteroids and vitamin D analogues, escalating to systemic or biologic therapy for severe disease
Correct systemic drivers such as hyperthyroidism, which produces the distal separation of Plummer's nail
Withdraw or substitute photosensitising drugs such as tetracyclines and psoralens and advise sun protection in photo-onycholysis
Treat secondary Pseudomonas colonisation causing greenish discolouration or coexisting candidal infection, and counsel that recovery is slow as it depends on outgrowth of attached plate
